segments.original: Canadians have to spend a lot of time patiently explaining that they are not American. Likewise, films made in Canada - with Toronto standing in for New York - are often hard to tell apart from those produced in the United States. This may be why certain Canadian directors make a point of creating works that set them apart from Hollywood's mainstream output.

segments.original: Even those whose careers have every so often taken them to the Los Angeles studios, such as David Cronenberg (b. 1943), resisted assimilation and continue to make unmistakably individual films, while the output of Canadian filmmakers such as Denys Arcand (b. 1941), Guy Maddin (b. 1956) and Atom Egoyan (b. 1960) remains proudly and determinedly idiosyncratic.

segments.original: David Cronenberg started out making ultra-low-budget underground films, but carried his recurring theme of "body horror" (body horror) into the sensationalist mainstream in productions such as his breakthrough film Shivers (1975). In it, as in the surreal Videodrome (1983), the theme of parasites and other elements that can invade the human body and turn against it becomes a metaphor for psychological and social dissolution.

segments.original: Atom Egoyan (b. 1960) likewise started small and moved progressively toward the mainstream. Drawing on his own Armenian-Canadian background and his family's turbulent history, he made a series of films in the 1980s – among them Peep Show (1981) and Family Viewing (1987) - that dealt insistently with problems of ethnic identity, dysfunctional homes, broken homes, alienation, loss and death. Alongside these themes lies an uneasy fascination with the role of visual media in the modern world. His characters obsessively use film and video to reconstruct reality so that it fits their desires - identity takes the form of a charade. Egoyan himself commented: "My films are designed to make viewers self-conscious. I take pride in that."

segments.original: Unlike Cronenberg and Egoyan, Guy Maddin shows little interest in making films for the mainstream circuit. His debut feature, Tales from the Gimli Hospital (1988), was so strange it could almost be seen as an act of contempt, a retro pastiche of silent-film stylization, with minimal dialogue, full of incoherences that provoke the viewer with a crazy logic.

segments.original: Quebec filmmakers are naturally distinguished from their American colleagues by language, while at the same time remaining distant from and different to their European cousins so as not to be absorbed into the French-language circuit. Denys Arcand, the best-known French-Canadian director on the international scene, started out making short documentaries for the National Film Board of Canada, but his radical political positions and independent nature created tension with his bosses.

segments.original: His first three features, including Gina (1975), used the thriller to explore political themes, but his views aroused official suspicion, and for some years he was given few resources to work with. Arcand bounced back in grand style with Le déclin de l'empire américain (The Decline of the American Empire, 1986), which was nominated for an Oscar, as was his next film, Jésus de Montréal (Jesus of Montreal, 1989), an intensely ironic fable about an actor who plays Christ in the city's annual Passion play and discovers that the role is taking control of his life.

segments.original: The saddest decline in Canadian cinema was surely that of Claude Jutra (1930-1986). In 1971, he directed Mon oncle Antoine (1971), which received a shower of awards and was voted the best Canadian film of all time in 1984. But his subsequent work was disappointing. In the mid-1980s, he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, and he died in 1986 after disappearing from his home. When the St. Lawrence River thawed in April 1987, his body was found in its waters.
